docs.title: Enterprise LLM Fine-Tuning: GPT-J at Walmart
The Problem
docs.text:
HR support was overwhelmed. Walmart's HR team received 20,000+ employee queries daily across benefits, policies, leave requests, and payroll issues. The existing rule-based chatbot could only handle ~30% of queries accurately, routing the rest to human agents.

Business impact: Long wait times, frustrated employees, and HR team burnout. We needed an AI solution that could handle complex, conversational queries while maintaining accuracy.

docs.title: The Constraint
docs.text:
We couldn't use OpenAI's API due to data privacy regulations. Employee HR data (salaries, health info, performance reviews) is highly sensitive and cannot leave Walmart's infrastructure.

The requirement: Fine-tune an open-source LLM on GCP within Walmart's compliance boundaries, achieving production-grade quality with 40%+ accuracy improvement.

docs.title: The Challenge
docs.text: Building a production LLM system from scratch meant solving multiple problems: - Scale: Fine-tuning a 6B parameter model on multi-TB HR datasets - Accuracy: Entity resolution for 500K+ employees, thousands of policies - Latency: Sub-second inference for 20K daily interactions - Reliability: Production deployment with monitoring and fallback systems

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
I architected a GPT-J (6B parameter) fine-tuning framework deployed on GCP, processing multi-TB HR datasets with PySpark and achieving production deployment with sub-second latency.

graph LR
    A[Internal HR Data] --> B[PySpark ETL]
    B --> C[Training Dataset]
    C --> D[GPT-J Fine-Tuning]
    D --> E[Model Validation]
    E --> F[GCP Deployment]
    F --> G[HR Chatbot API]
    G --> H[20K+ Daily Users]

docs.title: Challenge 1: Fitting 6B Parameters in GPU Memory
docs.text:
Problem: GPT-J has 6 billion parameters (~24GB in FP32). Even with GCP's A100 GPUs (40GB), we couldn't fit the model + optimizer states + gradients + batch data in memory.

Solution - Multi-pronged optimization strategy:

  1. DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 2: Sharded optimizer states across GPUs, reducing per-GPU memory by 50% 

    # DeepSpeed configuration
{
  "zero_optimization": {
    "stage": 2,  # Shard optimizer states
    "offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"},  # Offload to CPU RAM
    "allgather_bucket_size": 5e8,
    "reduce_bucket_size": 5e8
  },
  "fp16": {"enabled": true}  # Mixed precision
}

  2. Gradient Checkpointing: Trade compute for memory by recomputing activations during backward pass instead of storing them

  3. Reduced activation memory by ~70%

  4. Increased training time by only ~20% (acceptable trade-off)

  5. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): Instead of fine-tuning all 6B parameters, we injected trainable low-rank matrices

  6. Only 0.6B trainable parameters (10% of original)
  7. 90% reduction in GPU memory for gradients
  8. Minimal quality degradation vs full fine-tuning

Result: Fit the entire training pipeline on 4x A100 GPUs with batch size of 32.

docs.title: Challenge 2: Data Pipeline at Multi-TB Scale
docs.text:
Processing internal HR data (employee records, policies, support tickets, FAQs) across 10+ years:

PySpark Pipeline (distributed across 20-node cluster): 

# Conceptual - actual code simplified
training_data = (
    spark.read.parquet("hr_data_lake")
    .filter(col("year") >= 2018)  # Recent data only
    .join(policies, on="policy_id")
    .withColumn("prompt", create_prompt_udf(col("query")))
    .withColumn("completion", col("resolution"))
    .repartition(500)  # Distribute across workers
    .write.parquet("training_dataset")
)

Data processing innovations: - Deduplication: Fuzzy matching to remove near-duplicate queries (reduced dataset by 40%) - Augmentation: Synthetic query generation for edge cases (increased coverage by 25%) - Quality scoring: ML-based filtering to remove low-quality support tickets

Impact: Reduced preprocessing from 3 weeks to 2 days.

docs.title: Challenge 3: Production Deployment with Hot-Swapping
docs.text:
Requirement: Zero-downtime deployment for model updates (weekly retraining).

Solution - Blue/Green Deployment with GKE: 1. Deploy new model version to "green" cluster 2. Run shadow traffic (real queries, responses logged but not served) 3. Compare quality metrics (BLEU, entity accuracy) against "blue" production 4. Gradual traffic shift: 10% → 50% → 100% over 24 hours 5. Automatic rollback if error rate > 5%

Monitoring stack: - Latency: P50, P95, P99 inference times (target: P95 < 800ms) - Quality: Daily BERT-score evaluation on random sample - Drift: Feature distribution KL-divergence vs training data

docs.title: Data Engineering Pipeline

Built end-to-end data pipeline using PySpark to: - Process multi-TB datasets from internal HR systems (Workday, SuccessFactors, internal tools) - Clean and normalize employee records, policies, and FAQs - Generate high-quality training pairs with prompt engineering - Implement quality checks: duplicate detection, PII masking, data validation

Impact metric: Reduced data preprocessing time from weeks to days with distributed Spark processing.

docs.title: Operational Anomaly Detection at Scale
docs.text: Role: Senior Machine Learning Engineer | Tech Stack: Python, Scikit-Learn (Isolation Forest), Airflow, BigQuery

docs.title: 🚀 Executive Summary
docs.text: Designed and implemented an unsupervised anomaly detection system to identify operational irregularities and compliance risks across a distributed workforce. The system processed millions of weekly transaction events, moving the organization from reactive auditing to proactive, automated risk detection.

docs.title: 📉 The Challenge
docs.text: The organization relied on static, rule-based logic to monitor workforce scheduling and attendance. This approach generated high false-positive rates and failed to capture complex behavioral anomalies, such as: * Coordinated Irregularities: Patterns indicating potential collusion or process circumvention. * Systemic Deviations: Shifts in operational behavior that signaled training gaps or system misuse. * Scale Constraints: The solution needed to process high-velocity logs across thousands of locations within strict SLA windows.

docs.title: 🛠 The Solution
docs.text: I architected an Unsupervised Learning Pipeline capable of establishing baseline "normal" behavior for individual entities without requiring labeled fraud data.

docs.title: 1. Feature Engineering Strategy
docs.text: Instead of using hard-coded thresholds, I focused on extracting behavioral metadata to model intent: * Temporal Velocity: Analyzing the distribution of time deltas between interactions to identify non-human speeds. * Contextual Variance: Comparing individual activity against peer-group clusters (e.g., "Location A vs. Regional Average"). * Device Fingerprinting: Aggregating metadata to detect multi-user anomalies on single endpoints.

docs.title: 2. The Architecture
docs.text:
• Ingestion: Built a batch-processing framework using Airflow to ingest raw logs from the data lake.
  • Modeling: Utilized Isolation Forests for high-dimensional outlier detection, chosen for its efficiency with tabular data and resistance to masking.
  • Scalability: Optimized the pipeline using BigQuery partitioning and vectorization, reducing processing time by ~60% compared to legacy scripts.

docs.title: 3. Human-in-the-Loop Feedback
docs.text: To manage false positives, I designed a feedback workflow: * The model output a probabilistic risk score (0.0 - 1.0). * High-confidence anomalies were surfaced to operational leads. * A "Dismiss/Verify" signal was captured to dynamically adjust feature weights for future retraining cycles.

docs.title: 📊 Impact & Results
docs.text:
• Financial Impact: Projected 7-figure annual savings through the reduction of operational leakage and payroll errors.
  • Efficiency: Reduced manual audit time by ~20% by prioritizing high-risk cases over random sampling.
  • Operational Integrity: Successfully identified and remediated a specific class of "Ghost Shift" anomalies that had previously gone undetected by rule-based systems.

docs.title: Why Isolation Forest?
docs.text:
The Problem with Supervised Learning: We didn't have labeled "fraud" examples. Most operational irregularities are rare (<<1% of transactions), making it impractical to manually label millions of events.

Isolation Forest Advantage: - Works on the assumption that anomalies are "few and different" - O(n log n) complexity - scales to millions of records - No need for distance metrics (unlike KNN/LOF)

# Conceptual implementation
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

# Train on "normal" behavior baseline
model = IsolationForest(
    contamination=0.02,  # Expect ~2% anomalies
    n_estimators=200,
    max_samples=10000,
    random_state=42
)

# Fit on peer-group normalized features
model.fit(feature_matrix)

# Score new transactions
anomaly_scores = model.decision_function(new_transactions)

docs.title: Feature Engineering Details
docs.text:
Temporal Features: - Rolling 7-day, 30-day average activity patterns - Hour-of-day and day-of-week clustering - Time delta variance (coefficient of variation)

Contextual Features: - Z-scores relative to location/department peer groups - Device diversity metrics (unique device count per user) - Velocity flags (actions per minute, per hour)

Why this mattered: Raw timestamp data alone would flag night-shift workers as anomalies. Peer-group normalization distinguished "abnormal for this context" from "working nights."

docs.title: The Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
graph TB
    A[Data Lake] --> B[Airflow DAG]
    B --> C[BigQuery: Feature Engineering]
    C --> D[Isolation Forest Model]
    D --> E{Risk Score}
    E -->|High Risk| F[Alert Queue]
    E -->|Low Risk| G[Analytics DB]
    F --> H[Operational Review]
    H --> I[Feedback Loop]
    I --> D

Why Airflow: - Needed orchestration for multi-stage ETL (raw logs → features → scoring) - Required retry logic for flaky upstream data sources - SLA monitoring: pipeline had to complete within 4-hour window

Why BigQuery: - Petabyte-scale workforce data required columnar storage - SQL-based feature engineering was faster to iterate than PySpark - Partitioning by date reduced query costs by 80%

docs.title: Handling False Positives
docs.text:
The Business Constraint: Operational leads couldn't review 10,000 alerts per week. We needed <300 high-confidence alerts.

Solution - Tiered Alerting: 1. Auto-Dismiss: Score < 0.3 (baseline noise) 2. Watch List: 0.3 - 0.6 (logged for pattern analysis) 3. Manual Review: 0.6 - 0.8 (sent to supervisors) 4. Critical Escalation: > 0.8 (compliance team involved)

Feedback Loop: - Supervisors marked alerts as "True Positive" or "False Positive" - Weekly retraining adjusted feature weights using this signal - Over 6 months: False positive rate dropped from 35% → 12%

docs.title: 1. Anomaly Detection ≠ Fraud Detection
docs.text: Early versions of the model flagged legitimate edge cases (e.g., employees covering emergency shifts). We had to build context awareness into features rather than relying on raw counts.

docs.title: 2. Explainability Matters for Adoption
docs.text: Even though Isolation Forest is a "black box," we added SHAP values to show which features drove high anomaly scores. This built trust with operational teams who needed to action the alerts.

docs.title: 3. Cold Start Problem
docs.text: New employees had no "baseline" behavior for the first 30 days. Solution: Used location-level averages as a prior until enough individual data accumulated.

docs.text:

docs.title: GLORA: Global Events Analysis with LangChain
docs.text:
Conversational Intelligence for Global Events Data

View on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
GLORA (Global ??? Analysis) is a powerful tool for analyzing and querying global events using natural language. It combines LangChain's conversational AI capabilities with vector embeddings to provide semantic search and conversational analysis of event datasets.

Designed for researchers, analysts, and developers who need to extract insights from massive global event datasets without writing complex SQL queries or manual data analysis.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Global event databases contain millions of records with complex relationships. Traditional analysis requires:

  • Deep knowledge of database schemas
  • Complex SQL queries for pattern matching
  • Manual correlation of related events
  • Time-consuming exploratory data analysis

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
A natural language interface powered by LangChain and vector embeddings that allows users to:

  • Ask questions in plain English: "What events in Africa involved cybersecurity in 2023?"
  • Get semantic matches: Understands synonyms and related concepts
  • Conversational follow-ups: Build on previous queries with context
  • Fast vector search: Millions of records in milliseconds

    A[User Query] --> B[LangChain Agent]
    B --> C{Query Type}
    C -->|Semantic| D[Vector DB Search]
    C -->|Structured| E[SQL Query]

    G --> H[Response Generation]

docs.text:

  4. Indexing: Store in vector DB with metadata filters
  5. Retrieval: Hybrid search (vector + keyword + filters)

docs.title: LangChain Ollama Conversational Agent
docs.text:
Privacy-First AI Assistant with Tool-Augmented Reasoning

View on GitHub 1 Star

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A production-grade conversational agent that runs entirely on your local machine. Built with LangChain and Ollama, it combines the power of large language models with practical tools like web search, weather, and date retrieval - all without sending your data to the cloud.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Cloud-based AI services have limitations:

  • 💰 Expensive: API costs add up quickly with usage
  • 🔒 Privacy risks: Your conversations and data leave your machine
  • 🌐 Internet dependency: Requires constant connectivity
  • 📊 Data concerns: Your prompts may be used for training

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
Run powerful LLMs locally with tool integration:

  • ✅ Zero API costs after initial setup
  • ✅ Complete data privacy - everything stays on your machine
  • ✅ Works offline (except for tools requiring internet)
  • ✅ Full control over model selection and parameters

docs.text:
graph TB
    A[User Input] --> B[Streamlit UI]
    B --> C[LangChain Agent]

    E --> G[DuckDuckGo Search]

docs.title: Tool-Augmented Reasoning
docs.text:
The agent can invoke external tools when needed:

Tool Purpose Example Query DuckDuckGo Search Web search for current information "What's the latest news about AI?" Weather Real-time weather data "What's the weather in San Diego?" Date/Time Current date and time "What day of the week is it?"

The agent intelligently decides when to use tools vs when to answer from its internal knowledge.

docs.title: Agent Design
docs.text:
ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) pattern:

  1. Thought: Agent reasons about what to do
  2. Action: Decides to use a tool or answer directly
  3. Observation: Processes tool output
  4. Final Answer: Generates response
# Example agent reasoning
Thought: User wants weather info, I need to use the weather tool
Action: weather("San Diego")
Observation: Temperature: 72°F, Conditions: Sunny
Final Answer: It's currently 72°F and sunny in San Diego!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A comprehensive educational implementation of neural networks using only Python and NumPy - no deep learning frameworks. This project progressively builds from a single neuron to multi-layer networks with various optimization algorithms, providing deep insights into how neural networks actually work under the hood.

docs.title: The Learning Journey
docs.text:
Understanding neural networks at a fundamental level requires going beyond high-level APIs. This project deliberately avoids TensorFlow and PyTorch to expose the mathematical foundations:

  • Forward propagation: How inputs transform into predictions
  • Backpropagation: The calculus behind learning
  • Optimization: Different strategies for updating weights
  • Regularization: Preventing overfitting

docs.text: The implementation follows a progressive complexity approach, with each module building on the previous:

docs.title: Level 2: Single Layer

docs.title: Level 3: Multi-Layer Networks

docs.title: Forward Propagation
docs.text:
# Simple forward pass (conceptual)
def forward(X, weights, bias):
    # Linear transformation
    z = np.dot(X, weights) + bias
    # Activation (ReLU)
    a = np.maximum(0, z)
    return a

docs.title: Backpropagation
docs.text:
The chain rule in action:

∂Loss/∂weight = ∂Loss/∂output × ∂output/∂z × ∂z/∂weight

Each module implements this manually to reveal the mathematics.

docs.title: Optimizer Comparison
docs.text: Optimizer Learning Rate Momentum Adaptive Best For SGD Fixed ❌ ❌ Simple problems Momentum Fixed ✅ ❌ Smooth convergence AdaGrad Adaptive ❌ ✅ Sparse gradients RMSprop Adaptive ❌ ✅ Non-stationary Adam Adaptive ✅ ✅ General purpose

docs.title: Mathematical Foundations
docs.text:
Activation Functions:

  • ReLU: f(x) = max(0, x)
  • Sigmoid: f(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-x))
  • Tanh: f(x) = (e^x - e^(-x)) / (e^x + e^(-x))

Loss Functions:

  • MSE: L = (1/n) Σ(y - ŷ)²
  • Cross-Entropy: L = -Σ y·log(ŷ)

Regularization:

  • L1: R = λΣ|w| (encourages sparsity)
  • L2: R = λΣw² (prevents large weights)

docs.text:
1. Why backpropagation works: Not just what, but why
  2. Gradient flow: How gradients propagate through layers
  3. Vanishing gradients: Why deep networks are challenging
  4. Optimization landscape: Local minima, saddle points

docs.title: Part-of-Speech Tagging
docs.text:
NLP Project for Linguistic Analysis

View on GitHub 1 Star

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
An implementation of Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging for natural language processing. This project demonstrates core NLP techniques for analyzing text structure and extracting linguistic patterns.

POS tagging is a fundamental NLP task that assigns grammatical categories (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) to each word in a sentence, enabling downstream applications like named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and machine translation.

docs.title: What is POS Tagging?
docs.text:
Part-of-Speech tagging labels each word with its grammatical role:

Example:

Input:  "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
Output: DET ADJ  ADJ   NOUN VERB PREP DET ADJ  NOUN
        The quick brown fox  jumps over the  lazy dog

docs.title: Common POS Tags
docs.text: Tag Category Examples NOUN Noun dog, city, happiness VERB Verb run, think, is ADJ Adjective quick, brown, lazy ADV Adverb quickly, very, often DET Determiner the, a, this PREP Preposition in, on, over PRON Pronoun he, she, they CONJ Conjunction and, or, but

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
This project likely implements one or more of these approaches:

graph TD
    A[Input Sentence] --> B{POS Tagger Type}
    B -->|Rule-Based| C[Dictionary Lookup]
    B -->|Statistical| D[HMM/CRF Model]
    B -->|Neural| E[Deep Learning]
    C --> F[POS Sequence]
    D --> F
    E --> F

    style B fill:#667eea,stroke:#764ba2,stroke-width:3px,color:#fff
    style F fill:#2dd4bf,stroke:#14b8a6,stroke-width:2px

docs.text:
1. Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
  2. Probabilistic sequence model
  3. Learns transition and emission probabilities

  4. Fast and interpretable

  5. Conditional Random Fields (CRF)

  6. Discriminative sequence model
  7. Better handles feature dependencies

  8. Higher accuracy than HMM

  9. Neural Networks

  10. BiLSTM or Transformer-based
  11. Captures long-range dependencies
  12. State-of-the-art performance

docs.text:

"Apple Inc. released the iPhone"
NOUN  NOUN VERB    DET  NOUN

Nouns following proper nouns often indicate organizations.

  • Verbs indicate actions/opinions

docs.title: Ambiguity
docs.text:
Many words have multiple possible tags:

"Time flies like an arrow"
NOUN VERB  PREP DET NOUN   (intended meaning)
VERB NOUN  VERB DET NOUN   (alternative parse)

docs.title: Unknown Words
docs.text:
Handling words not seen during training:

  • Use morphological features (suffixes like -ing, -ed)
  • Context-based inference
  • Back-off to most common tag

docs.title: Domain Adaptation
docs.text:
Models trained on news may perform poorly on:

  • Social media text
  • Technical documentation
  • Informal speech

docs.title: YouTube Shorts AI Agent
docs.text:
Autonomous Content Generation with Multi-Agent Architecture

View on GitHub

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: An intelligent multi-agent system that transforms a simple topic request into a production-ready YouTube Shorts concept. Built with Google's Agent Developer Kit (ADK) and Gemini 2.0, it autonomously researches trends, writes scripts, validates viral potential, and generates detailed visual directions.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Content creation is time-consuming and requires constant trend awareness. Creators spend hours researching what's trending, brainstorming ideas, writing scripts, and planning visuals. This agent automates the entire ideation process while ensuring the content has viral potential.

docs.title: The Solution
docs.text:
A sequential chain of specialized AI agents that collaborate to produce high-quality video concepts:

  1. Research trending topics using real-time Google Trends data
  2. Write initial script based on trending insights
  3. Validate viral potential through a quality scoring loop
  4. Refine script iteratively until it meets quality thresholds
  5. Visualize detailed shot-by-shot visual directions
  6. Format final output as production-ready markdown

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TD
    A[User Input: Topic] --> B[MemoryCoordinator]
    B --> C[Researcher Agent]
    C --> |Google Trends MCP| D[Get Trending Data]
    D --> E[ScriptWriter Agent]
    E --> F[Quality Loop]
    F --> G[StateInitializer]
    G --> H[ViralityJudge]
    H --> |Score < 8| I[ScriptRefiner]
    I --> |Iteration < 3| H
    H --> |Score ≥ 8| J[Exit Loop]
    J --> K[Visualizer Agent]
    K --> L[Formatter Agent]
    L --> M[Final Output: Production Plan]

    style F fill:#667eea,stroke:#764ba2,stroke-width:3px,color:#fff
    style D fill:#f093fb,stroke:#764ba2,stroke-width:2px
    style M fill:#2dd4bf,stroke:#14b8a6,stroke-width:2px

docs.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
docs.text:
8 specialized agents working in sequence, each with a focused responsibility:

Agent Purpose Model MemoryCoordinator Future-ready context management gemini-2.0-flash Researcher Fetches trending topics via Google Trends MCP gemini-2.0-flash ScriptWriter Drafts initial script from trending insights gemini-2.0-flash StateInitializer Prevents context errors in quality loop gemini-2.0-flash ViralityJudge Scores content engagement (0-10 scale) gemini-2.0-flash ScriptRefiner Iterates based on feedback gemini-2.0-flash Visualizer Creates shot-by-shot visual direction gemini-2.0-flash-lite Formatter Produces markdown table output gemini-2.0-flash-lite

docs.title: Google Trends Integration via MCP
docs.text:
What is MCP?

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard for connecting AI models to external data sources. It allows agents to call custom tools and APIs in a standardized way.

This project implements a custom MCP server (mcp_server.py) that exposes Google Trends data:

  • Real-time trending searches from Google Trends RSS feed
  • Interest over time analysis
  • Related queries discovery
  • Async tool implementation for seamless ADK integration

The mcp_client_tool.py wraps the MCP server as an ADK FunctionTool, enabling the Researcher agent to access live trend data.

docs.title: Smart Quality Loop
docs.text:
A self-correcting mechanism ensures viral potential:

# Quality Loop Flow
while iterations < 3:
    score = ViralityJudge.evaluate(script)
    if score >= 8:
        exit_loop()  # Quality threshold met
    else:
        script = ScriptRefiner.improve(script, feedback)
  • Maximum 3 iterations to prevent infinite loops
  • Score threshold of 8/10 for viral potential
  • Automatic refinement based on structured feedback
  • Tool-based exit using exit_loop() function

docs.title: Tech Stack
docs.text:
• Google ADK - Agent orchestration framework
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash - LLM for tool-enabled agents
  • Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite - Optimized for text-only tasks
  • Python 3.11+ - Runtime environment
  • MCP - Model Context Protocol for Trends integration
  • Docker - Containerized deployment

docs.title: Agent Pipeline Design
docs.text:
Sequential orchestration prevents tool compatibility conflicts:

  1. Agents pass context via session state
  2. Clean separation of concerns
  3. No parallel tool usage conflicts
  4. Predictable execution flow

docs.title: Model Optimization
docs.text:
Strategic model selection for cost and performance:

  • gemini-2.0-flash: Agents with tools (Researcher, Refiner, StateInitializer)
  • gemini-2.0-flash-lite: Text-only agents (Visualizer, Formatter)

docs.text:
A complete production plan in markdown table format:

Beat Script Visual Direction Duration Opening Hook Attention-grabbing statement Close-up, dynamic text 3s Main Content Core message based on trends B-roll, graphics overlay 20s Call to Action Engagement prompt Face camera, subscribe prompt 7s

docs.title: Performance Metrics
docs.text:
• Research to output: ~30-45 seconds
  • Quality iterations: 1-3 cycles
  • Trend relevance: Real-time data
  • Viral potential: 8+/10 guaranteed

docs.title: Challenges Solved
docs.text:
1. Context Management: Implemented StateInitializer to prevent variable errors in quality loop
  2. Tool Compatibility: Used sequential orchestration to avoid function call conflicts
  3. Quality Assurance: Designed self-correction loop with exit conditions
  4. Trend Integration: Built custom MCP server for real-time data access

docs.text:

  • Why MCP? Standardized way to integrate external APIs with LLM agents
  • Why Quality Loop? Ensures consistent output quality without manual review
